2	
3	Read this when adding, upgrading, or pinning an action or reusable workflow, when configuring

5

18	## Pin to a commit SHA
19	
20	`uses: some-org/some-action@v1` resolves a tag, and a tag is a pointer the action's maintainer, or
21	anyone who compromises their account, can move. The `tj-actions/changed-files` compromise in March
22	2025 worked exactly this way: existing tags were repointed at a malicious commit, and thousands of
23	repositories consumed it on their next run without changing a line.
24	
25	```yaml
26	- uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
27	```
28	
29	- Use the full 40-character SHA. An abbreviated SHA is rejected.
30	- Keep the version in a trailing comment. Without it the reference is unreadable, and Dependabot
31	  uses the comment to propose updates.
32	- Pin the SHA of a commit that a release tag pointed to, not an arbitrary commit from the default
33	  branch.
34	- Verify the commit belongs to the repository named in `uses:`. A SHA from a fork can be reachable
35	  through the upstream repository's object store, so a reference that looks upstream can resolve to
36	  fork code.
37	
38	Actions published by GitHub itself (`actions/*`, `github/*`) carry lower risk than third-party ones,
39	but the reasoning is the same and the pinning rule is not worth making conditional.
40	
41	Immutable releases prevent a published release's tag and assets from being changed, and generate a
42	signed attestation for each asset. They are generally available and configurable per repository or
43	per organization, applying to releases published after the setting is turned on. They narrow the
44	window but do not close it: the protection covers the release's own tag, so the moving major or
45	minor tags most workflows reference, `@v1` and `@v1.2`, stay mutable because they are separate tags
46	that no release owns, and a repository that has not enabled the setting is unaffected. SHA pinning
47	remains the guidance.
48	
49	## Pin to the latest release
50	
51	Pinning and currency are separate requirements, and satisfying only the first produces the worst
52	outcome: an action frozen at a version whose known vulnerabilities are never fixed, with the pin
53	providing the appearance of control. A SHA pin is not a reason to stay on an old version; it is the
54	reason updating has to be deliberate.
55	
56	Whenever a `uses:` line is added or touched, resolve the action's current release rather than
57	carrying the version already in the file forward:
58	
59	```sh
60	gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/releases/latest --jq .tag_name
61	gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/commits/<tag> --jq .sha
62	```
63	
64	- Do not treat the version already in the workflow, or a version recalled from memory, as current.
65	  Look it up during the change.
66	- `releases/latest` excludes drafts and prereleases. Where a repository publishes tags without
67	  releases, take the newest tag from `gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/tags` and confirm against the
68	  repository that it is a release rather than a build or nightly marker.
69	- Read the release notes across every version being skipped, not only the newest. A major-version
70	  bump changes the runtime, inputs, or defaults often enough that it needs checking, and the
71	  reasoning belongs in the pull request description.
72	- Balance currency against the cooldown below. The newest release and a release old enough to be
73	  trusted are not always the same version; where they differ, prefer the newest release that clears
74	  the cooldown, and say which one was chosen.
75	- Where a version must stay behind, for example because a newer major drops a runner or an input the
76	  workflow depends on, state the reason in a comment on the line, so it is not read later as neglect.
77	
78	`pinact run -update` and `ratchet update` re-resolve every pinned reference to the current release,
79	and are the practical way to apply this across a repository. Both rewrite the files in place, so run
80	them on a clean tree and review the resulting diff; do not merge it unread. `pinact run -check`
81	reports what is unpinned without editing anything, which is the form to use in CI or when a
82	confirmed write is not wanted.
83	
84	## Pinning does not stop at `uses:`
85	
86	A pinned action can still fetch mutable content at run time. Before trusting one, read its
87	`action.yml` and any Dockerfile or shell script it ships, and look for:
88	
89	- `uses:` references inside a composite action that are themselves on a tag or branch
90	- `FROM ubuntu:latest` or any unpinned base image in a Docker action
91	- `curl ... | bash`, `wget`, or a download from a release URL that is not checksum-verified
92	- `npm install`, `pip install`, or `go install` without a lockfile or a pinned version
93	- Network calls to a host unrelated to the action's stated purpose
94	
95	Reusable workflows are third-party dependencies with the same properties. Pin
96	`uses: org/repo/.github/workflows/x.yml@<sha>` the same way.
97	
98	OpenSSF Scorecard's Pinned-Dependencies check scores the whole repository, not only workflow
99	`uses:` lines. It reads Dockerfile `FROM` lines and `curl` or `wget` downloads in shipped scripts,
100	in addition to the workflow `uses:` lines above, and scores the fraction pinned to a hash. A full
101	semantic version for a Go module counts as pinned; everything else needs a digest. Package
102	manifests and their lock files are not part of what this check reads, but commit them for every
103	ecosystem that supports them regardless, since they are what makes a build reproducible. A
104	repository chasing that check pins its base images by `sha256` and checksum-verifies scripted
105	downloads, alongside the action pinning above.
106	
107	## Choosing an action at all
108	
109	The safest action is the one not added. A three-line `run:` step often replaces a dependency that
110	brings an unaudited JavaScript bundle into a job holding the repository token.
111	
112	When one is warranted, check: whether the source is readable and small, whether it is actively
113	maintained, whether the publisher is a verified creator or a known organization, and whether the
114	name is a near-match for a more popular action, which is how typosquatting works. Prefer forking a
115	critical action into the organization and pinning that, so an upstream compromise does not propagate
116	automatically.
117	
118	## Dependabot
119	
120	```yaml
121	version: 2
122	updates:
123	  - package-ecosystem: github-actions
124	    directory: /
125	    schedule:
126	      interval: weekly
127	    cooldown:
128	      default-days: 7
129	```
130	
131	- Dependabot updates SHA pins and rewrites the version comment, so pinning does not freeze a
132	  repository at an old version. It is what keeps the latest-release rule true between changes, rather
133	  than only at the moment someone edits the file, so configure it in any repository that pins.
134	- A cooldown, `cooldown` for Dependabot or `minimumReleaseAge` for Renovate, delays adoption of a
135	  brand-new release. Most malicious releases are found and yanked within days, so a delay of about a
136	  week absorbs a large share of the risk at little cost.
137	- Security alerts for actions are generated from semantic versions. A SHA-pinned action receives
138	  version-update pull requests but may not raise an alert, so the update pull requests must actually
139	  be reviewed and merged rather than left open.
140	- Review a Dependabot action bump by reading the upstream diff between the two SHAs, not by trusting
141	  the version number.

143	## Policy enforcement
144	
145	Set these at the organization or enterprise level, in Settings, Actions, Policies. They apply to
146	every repository regardless of what a workflow file says:

content.text:
**A full-SHA pin doesn't prove the commit belongs to the repository named in `uses:`, and GitHub's commits API won't tell you either.** I asked it for the fork commit from Chainguard's post under `actions/checkout`, and for the Trivy imposter prefix `70379aad`. Both resolved.

## How it works
Forks share Git object storage with their parent, so a commit pushed to any fork can be fetched by SHA through the parent's name. `uses: actions/checkout@<fork-sha>` therefore runs attacker code that looks upstream, and passes both an `actions/*` allowlist and "require full-length SHA".

The attacker still has to **get that SHA into a workflow or tag**, through an accepted PR, stolen write access or a compromised dependency. A correct existing pin can't be redirected this way.

## The two articles
**[Chainguard](https://www.chainguard.dev/unchained/what-the-fork-imposter-commits-in-github-actions-and-ci-cd) (March 2023)** is the substantive one.
- It explains the mechanism and calls it a form of dependency confusion.
- It reports no known exploitation at the time, after a non-exhaustive search.
- It offers a checker, `clank`, and notes that signing is only a partial answer.
- It predates both the 2026 incidents and lockfiles.

**[The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/hackers-found-way-around-github-sha.html) (24 November 2026)** is a contributed piece promoting a webinar by a Chainguard speaker. It has no IOCs, commit SHAs, detection steps or source links.
- **The technique isn't new:** "found way around" describes something published in 2023.
- **Trivy is misleadingly compressed:** it says teams pinned to the commit "would have passed every check". Other reporting says the attacker [committed the imposter pin into Trivy's own release workflow](https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy/security/advisories/GHSA-69fq-xp46-6x23), and separately [force-pushed 76 of 77 `trivy-action` tags](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2026-33634).
- **`actions-cool/issues-helper`:** I found only [one secondary mention](https://www.ajayk.sh/blog/github-actions-security-2026-supply-chain/), so treat its details as unconfirmed.

## What lockfiles change
They [became generally available on 28 October](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-28-github-actions-workflow-lockfiles-are-generally-available/), and are the first platform control here that addresses fork commits. According to the [docs](https://docs.github.com/actions/concepts/security/workflow-dependency-lockfiles), a locked commit that exists only in a fork is rejected at run time. I haven't tested that.

Limits:
- Only onboarded workflows are covered, unless the "Require lockfile" policy is active.
- Reusable workflow calls (`jobs.<id>.uses`) aren't locked.
- `./` local actions aren't locked without migrating them to `$/`.
- They don't judge whether a dependency is safe.
- The news piece says GitHub Enterprise Server isn't supported; the docs pages read didn't say.

## Checking a pin
All six distinct versioned pins in this repo's workflows match the tag in their version comment. The check for each:

```sh
gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/commits/refs/tags/TAG --jq .sha   # must equal the pinned SHA
```

- **A match** shows the upstream repository's tag points there. It doesn't help if the attacker moved the tag.
- **`compare/main...SHA`** returned `diverged` for the fork commit. Legitimate release-branch commits can do the same, so it can't decide on its own.
- **`zizmor`** has an `impostor-commit` online audit, as far as I recall. I didn't test it; running `GH_TOKEN=... uvx zizmor@1.31.1 <workflow>` on a file with a known fork SHA would confirm it.

## Gaps in this repo
`skills/github/github-actions-security/references/supply-chain.md`:
1. **No verification method:** lines 34-36 say to verify the commit belongs to the repository but not how. Add the tag-match command and warn that `commits/<sha>` succeeding proves nothing.
2. **No lockfiles:** neither the pinning nor the policy section mentions them.
3. **Overstated policy control:** line 153 says required SHA pinning "makes SHA pinning an invariant". That's true, but it should add that it doesn't check where the commit came from.

I'd fix 1 and 3 now, since they're small and tested. Item 2 should be a separate change, because adopting lockfiles also affects allowlists, Dependabot and CI. I haven't edited anything.

## Pin to a commit SHA

`uses: some-org/some-action@v1` resolves a tag, and a tag is a pointer the action's maintainer, or
anyone who compromises their account, can move. The `tj-actions/changed-files` compromise in March
2025 worked exactly this way: existing tags were repointed at a malicious commit, and thousands of
repositories consumed it on their next run without changing a line.

```yaml
- uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
```

- Use the full 40-character SHA. An abbreviated SHA is rejected.
- Keep the version in a trailing comment. Without it the reference is unreadable, and Dependabot
  uses the comment to propose updates.
- Pin the SHA of a commit that a release tag pointed to, not an arbitrary commit from the default
  branch.
- Verify the commit belongs to the repository named in `uses:`. A SHA from a fork can be reachable
  through the upstream repository's object store, so a reference that looks upstream can resolve to
  fork code, called an imposter commit.

To check a pin, resolve the tag in its version comment and compare the result with the pinned SHA:

```sh
gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/commits/refs/tags/TAG --jq .sha
```

- A successful `repos/OWNER/REPO/commits/<sha>` lookup proves nothing, because it also returns
  commits that exist only in a fork.
- A mismatch is unresolved, not proof of an attack: a moving tag such as `v4` advances past older
  pins. Check the full release tag, and do not accept the pin until its origin is established.
- A match shows only that the upstream tag points at that commit now. It does not detect a tag that
  an attacker moved.

Actions published by GitHub itself (`actions/*`, `github/*`) carry lower risk than third-party ones,
but the reasoning is the same and the pinning rule is not worth making conditional.

Immutable releases prevent a published release's tag and assets from being changed, and generate a
signed attestation for each asset. They are generally available and configurable per repository or
per organization, applying to releases published after the setting is turned on. They narrow the
window but do not close it: the protection covers the release's own tag, so the moving major or
minor tags most workflows reference, `@v1` and `@v1.2`, stay mutable because they are separate tags
that no release owns, and a repository that has not enabled the setting is unaffected. SHA pinning
remains the guidance.

## Pin to the latest release

Pinning and currency are separate requirements, and satisfying only the first produces the worst
outcome: an action frozen at a version whose known vulnerabilities are never fixed, with the pin
providing the appearance of control. A SHA pin is not a reason to stay on an old version; it is the
reason updating has to be deliberate.

Whenever a `uses:` line is added or touched, resolve the action's current release rather than
carrying the version already in the file forward:

```sh
gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/releases/latest --jq .tag_name
gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/commits/<tag> --jq .sha
```

- Do not treat the version already in the workflow, or a version recalled from memory, as current.
  Look it up during the change.
- `releases/latest` excludes drafts and prereleases. Where a repository publishes tags without
  releases, take the newest tag from `gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/tags` and confirm against the
  repository that it is a release rather than a build or nightly marker.

### The grader review gate

An assertion of kind `workspace_command` is handed to a shell by `run_grader`, in a process whose
HOME holds a symlink to the credentials that authenticate the run. Whoever writes that string
chooses what runs on this machine. `tasks`, `agent-tasks` and `regrade`, the three subcommands
that execute one, therefore refuse to start when a suite's `assertions.json`, `tasks.json`,
`fixtures/` or `patches/`, or `run_eval.py`, differs from `origin/main`, falling back to `main`:

```sh
python3 evals/run_eval.py tasks --skill python-testing
# refusing to grade python-testing: 1 grader-bearing path(s) differ from origin/main
```

The refusal lists every path that differs and the `workspace_command` strings that are new or
changed against the baseline, which is what a review of them consists of. Read those, then pass
`--graders-reviewed` to proceed. `instructions-tasks` carries the gate too.
The comparison is against the working tree rather than `HEAD`, so it covers a contributor's branch
and a patch applied locally alike, and it fires on uncommitted edits to a suite of one's own. That
is the intended cost: the flag is an assertion that a human read the commands, and it is recorded
in the run's output when it is used.

The freshness check compares revisions rather than dates. A run writes the commit it measured
to `results/raw/<stamp>/source-revision.json`, and the check asks `git merge-base

change committed later on the day of the run carries the same date as the stamp, and a commit
rebased or cherry-picked forward carries an author date older than the day it landed. Stamps
written before the run recorded a revision, and stamps whose revision a history rewrite
removed, fall back to comparing the committer date against the stamp name, and the finding
says which comparison produced it.

that graded a modified tree is reported on its own, because the source it measured is in no
commit: the revision it recorded is a lower bound rather than a record, and the comparison
above can still prove a change came afterwards but cannot prove the run included one. Commit
before measuring, and the finding does not arise.

    `EVAL_TOOL_BIN` lets the caller provision `ansible-lint`, `zizmor`, or
    `actionlint` outside the user's own PATH and still have runs find them. Passing

    loses every GitHub token and gh config variable, so neither an agent nor a grader reaches
    real GitHub.
    """
    env = dict(os.environ)
    if home is not None:
        # A token inherited from the caller's shell would let an agent act on real GitHub.
        for name in FORGE_TOKEN_VARIABLES:
            env.pop(name, None)
    tool_bin = env.get("EVAL_TOOL_BIN")
    if tool_bin:
        env["PATH"] = f"{tool_bin}{os.pathsep}{env['PATH']}"
    if home is not None:
        env = {
            name: value
            for name, value in env.items()
            if not name.startswith("CLAUDE") or name in INHERITED_CLAUDE_VARIABLES
        }
        env.update(isolated_environment(home))
        stub = home / GH_STUB_HOME
        if (stub / "bin").is_dir():
            env["GH_STUB_DIR"] = str(stub)

## How a task eval works

Each task runs twice against an identical copy of its fixture. The only difference between
the two runs is a single-skill plugin passed with `--plugin-dir`, built from the skill under
test plus `instructions/`, exactly as a real plugin install would resolve. Both runs load
`--setting-sources project` so the user's own settings and installed plugins stay out of
both arms. The result is that any difference is attributable to the skill, and `skills_used`
in each `grade.json` records whether it actually fired.

Neither that flag nor the per-run `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` keeps out an instruction file sitting in
an ancestor of the run directory, because Claude Code walks up from its working directory and
loads `CLAUDE.md`, `CLAUDE.local.md` and `.claude/CLAUDE.md` wherever it finds them. A checkout
under `$HOME` has `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` as such an ancestor, and ten transcripts across the
2026-09-13 stamps, in both conditions, end on wording taken from one. A probe on 2026-10-06,
with a private `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` and `--setting-sources project`, quoted that file when run
from `evals/` and found nothing when run from `/tmp`. `tasks`, `triggers` and `agent-tasks`
therefore refuse to start while any of those files exists above `evals/`. Run from a checkout
outside those directories, or pass `--allow-ancestor-instructions` to measure anyway, in which
case the paths are recorded in `source-revision.json` and the rendered report states that the
baseline ran with that guidance.

`AGENTS.md` takes a different route. Claude Code loads it through a builtin plugin,
`cc-plugin-agents-md`, from the working directory or an ancestor, and only where the project has
no `CLAUDE.md`. That spares the `doc` and `plain` arms and exposes every other condition, so this
repository's own `AGENTS.md` was loaded into the baseline arm of the 2026-10-20 minimal-change
stamp. Refusing to start would rule out every run from a checkout of this repository, so each run
disables the plugin through `--settings` instead, and the harness stops when a transcript shows it
loaded anyway. `evals/minimal-change/incidents/baseline-reads-checkout.md` holds the evidence.

The caller's environment is the third route. A harness started from inside a Claude Code session
inherits that session's variables, and they reach every run: from a cloud session on 2026-10-24,
a run picked up two of the session's skills and three event types its transcript would not
otherwise contain. Each run therefore drops every variable whose name starts with `CLAUDE`, except
the provider, credential, and mTLS variables listed in `INHERITED_CLAUDE_VARIABLES` in
`run_eval.py`. A provider variable missing from that list fails a run at authentication rather
than changing it quietly. The stamps from 2026-09-13 to 2026-10-20 were all started from inside a
session and show neither effect, which rules out those two and not a setting a transcript does
not record, such as the reasoning effort.

Assertions are of two kinds, and neither asks for a judgment: a `workspace_command` runs in
the finished workspace and passes on exit 0, and a regex kind matches against the run's
transcript, its Bash commands, or its final message. Each carries a `source` field naming the
line of the skill it comes from. `$EVAL_BASE_SHA` is exported to every grading command as the
commit the fixture started at, so "which files did this run change" is answerable.

A task run acts on its workspace without a permission prompt, because `claude -p` cannot
answer one and a denied call would be recorded as a skill that did not act. What bounds the
run is therefore the tool list rather than the permission mode: `TASK_TOOLS` in
`run_eval.py` allows Bash, the file tools, and `Skill`, and nothing else. A fixture is
attacker-shaped input by construction, since every one of them plants the flaw its eval
measures, and the allowlist keeps a run that reads one from reaching the rest of the tool
surface. Pass `--all-tools` to measure a task against every tool the CLI offers instead.

    assertion: dict[str, Any], workspace: Path, facts: dict[str, Any], base_sha: str, home: Path

    """Grade one assertion, returning its verdict and the evidence behind it."""
    kind = assertion["kind"]

    return {
        "id": assertion["id"],
        "kind": kind,
        "source": assertion.get("source", ""),
        "passed": passed,
        "evidence": evidence.strip()[:4000],
